sections.title: The Prohibition of Entering and Approaching Houses of Idolatry
sections.html:
It is forbidden to enter houses of idolatrous worship, because the Torah forbade drawing near to idolatry and taking an interest in it, lest one be enticed after it, as it is stated: "Do not turn to the idols" (Vayikra 19:4). Because of the great importance and gravity of the matter, the Torah warned Israel again and again not to be enticed after idolatry, as it is stated: "Take great care for your souls… lest you lift up your eyes to the heavens and see the sun, the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them" (Devarim 4:15-19). And it is stated in the passage of Ve-haya Im Shamo'a (ibid. 11:16): "Beware lest your heart be enticed, and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow down to them." And it is stated: "Beware lest you be ensnared after them, after they have been destroyed before you, and lest you inquire after their gods, saying: How did these nations serve their gods? I too will do likewise" (Devarim 12:30).

One who enters a place of idolatry also neglects the Torah commandment to destroy and uproot the name of idolatry, as it is stated: "You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a banned thing" (ibid. 7:26), and it is stated: "You shall tear down their altars, smash their pillars, burn their asherim in fire, and cut down the carved images of their gods, and you shall destroy their name from that place" (ibid. 12:3). Included in the mitzva is to treat idolatry with contempt and disgust, and even to avoid mentioning its name (below 14:1); all the more so one must not enter its place of worship. If the one who enters also watches the worship, he resembles one who pays honour to it, like one who embraces and kisses an idol, and in this too he transgresses a prohibition (Igrot Moshe YD 2:111, based on Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:6).

One who enters a house of idolatry and enjoys seeing its images thereby also transgresses the prohibition of deriving benefit from idolatry (SA YD 142:15; see Ḥokhmat Adam 84:16; above 10:8).

The Sages instructed us to keep away from the entrance of a house of idolatry, as it is stated: "Keep your way far from her, and do not come near the door of her house" (Mishlei 5:8). The Sages expounded: ""Keep your way far from her" – this is heresy (minut); "and do not come near the door of her house" – this is the government (wicked rule)… or a harlot (a house of prostitution)." The same law applies to idolatry. One who needs to pass by the entrance of a house of idolatry or the entrance of a brothel is commanded to keep four amot away from them, in order to express his revulsion at them, and in order to remove from himself any shadow of suspicion that he desires to be near them (Avoda Zara 17a; SA YD 150:1). It is related of the Amoraim of the Land of Israel, Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yonatan, that they were walking on their way and had to choose between a road that passed by the entrance of a house of idolatry and a road that passed by the entrance of a brothel, and they chose to take the road that passed by the entrance of the brothel, because idolatry is worse (Avoda Zara 17b, Tosafot s.v. "Nezil"; and see Eruvin 18b: "Behind a woman, and not behind idolatry").

Included in the prohibition, it is forbidden to enter or approach the houses of worship of Christians, Hindus and Muslims. And although according to many Christianity and Hinduism are permitted to Noahides, since they associate [other powers] with belief in a supreme God, for Jews they are forbidden as idolatry, and therefore they are included in the Torah prohibition, "Do not turn to the idols" (Vayikra 19:4), and it is forbidden for Jews to enter their houses of worship. And although there is no idolatry in Islam, most Muslims today have chosen to hate Israel, and the Sages said (Sifrei Zuta, Bamidbar 10:35): "Whoever is an enemy and hater of Israel is as if he is an enemy and hater of the Omnipresent"; therefore there is a mitzva to keep away from them, as it is stated: "Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and do I not quarrel with those who rise up against You? I hate them with utmost hatred; they have become my enemies" (Tehillim 139:21-22) (below, section 5).

sections.title: The Prohibition of Walking on a Road That Leads to a Place of Worship
sections.html:
The Sages forbade walking on a road that leads to a house of idolatry at a time when worship is being held there, because of mar'it ayin (how things appear), lest one be suspected of going to take part in its worship or to honour it. Only if that road also leads to another place is it permitted to walk on it to the other place. Likewise, one who lives near there may walk on it to his home (Avoda Zara 11b; Rabbeinu Yona, Ra'avad, Rosh and others).

The Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 9:9-10) is very stringent in his interpretation of this law: in his opinion the Sages forbade entering a city in which there is a place of idolatry, and all the more so it is forbidden to live there; only when the road to another place passes through it is it permitted to pass through (as cited in the note). In practice, however, the halakha follows the view of most poskim, that the prohibition is to walk on a road that leads to a place of idolatry at a time when worship is being held there (SA YD 149:1-2).1

sections.title: Mar'it Ayin and the Courtyard of a House of Idolatry
sections.html:
Even for one who has no interest at all in idolatry, and even at a time when no worship is being held in the house of idolatry, it is forbidden to enter a house of idolatry because of mar'it ayin, so that he will not be suspected of wishing to draw near to idolatry and to worship it.

The poskim disagree whether it is permitted to enter the courtyard of a house of idolatry at a time when no worship is being held there. Some permit it, for example when one wishes to enter the courtyard to sit in the shade of the trees (Rabbeinu Yona, Rosh). Others forbid it, so that one will not be suspected of wishing to draw near to idolatry and to worship it; however, if the road passed through the courtyard of a house of idolatry, it is permitted to walk on it on one's way to another place (Rambam, Rashba). The custom follows the stringent opinion, and it is a measure of piety that even when the road passes through the courtyard of a house of idolatry, if there is an alternative route that is not longer, one refrains from taking the road that passes through the courtyard of the house of idolatry (Rema YD 149:2; Tzitz Eliezer 14:91:2; Igrot Moshe YD 3:129:6).

For one who is compelled to pass near a place of idolatry, the Sages instructed that he not do anything that looks as if he is bowing to it. Therefore, if a thorn became stuck in his foot or his coins scattered in front of idolatry, he should not bend down to remove the thorn or to gather the coins facing it, because he looks as if he is bowing to it. Rather, he should sit or bend down while turning his back or his side to the idolatry, and in this way remove the thorn and gather his coins. Even when there is no one there who sees him, he should not bend down with his face toward the idolatry, because anything that the Sages forbade because of mar'it ayin of a Torah prohibition is forbidden even in the innermost chambers. Similarly, the custom of idolaters was to set up in front of the idol faces in its likeness, through whose mouths they would make water flow, and the Sages forbade drinking from them, so that one should not appear to be kissing the idol. Similarly, if a spring flowed in front of idolatry, one should not bend down and drink from it, so that he will not appear to be bowing to the idolatry (Avoda Zara 12a; SA YD 150:2; Shakh 1).

Some say that even in a situation of mortal danger from thirst, one should not drink in a manner that looks like bowing to idolatry. Many hold that since the prohibition is only because of mar'it ayin, in a situation of pikuaḥ nefesh (danger to life) he should drink, even though he looks as if he is bowing to the image. And this is the halakha (Ran; Rema YD 150:3). Therefore, one who is being pursued by someone seeking to kill him may enter a house of idolatry even during worship, since he is entering there to save his life.2

sections.title: A Christian Church
sections.html:
As we learned (above 5:7, 10), although according to most poskim Christianity is idolatry with shituf, which is permitted to Noahides, for Jews it is considered idolatry. Therefore, it is included in the Torah prohibition, "Do not turn to the idols" (Vayikra 19:4): it is forbidden for a Jew to enter a Christian church, and likewise one must keep away from the entrance of a church as from the entrance of a house of idolatry (above, section 1). A Jew who enjoys seeing its images, hearing the music played in its honour or smelling the incense burned before it also transgresses the prohibition of benefiting from idolatry (above 10:8). It is even forbidden to walk on a road that leads to a church at a time when worship is being held in it, so that one will not be suspected of going to take part in their worship (above, section 2).

In addition, Christianity, which aroused hatred of Israel and tried to make Jews abandon their religion, was considered minut, that is, a view that endangers Jews and Judaism. As halakha, one must keep away from a house of minut as from a house of idolatry, as it is stated: "And do not stray after your heart" (Bamidbar 15:39); the Sages expounded: ""After your heart" – this is minut" (Sifrei ad loc.; Berakhot 12b). It is also stated: "Keep your way far from her, and do not come near the door of her house" (Mishlei 5:8); the Sages expounded (Avoda Zara 17a): ""Keep your way far from her" – this is minut…."

In recent generations, many changes for the better have taken place among Christians. First, in a gradual process the idolatrous aspect has weakened, to the point that some poskim hold that it is no longer considered idolatry (above 5:12). However, most poskim hold that as long as Christians believe that "that man" is God, it is idolatry with shituf. Second, many Christians have renounced hatred of Israel. The leaders of the Catholic stream adopted a decision in principle expressing opposition to hatred of Israel and to missionary activity among Jews, and some of them even said that the divine election of Israel has not been annulled. Likewise, within the Protestant stream, evangelical movements of lovers of Israel have formed, who believe in the special quality of Israel and even assisted the Zionist movement, such as Lord Balfour (above 6:7-8, n. 3). All who share these positions are not considered minim, and many of them are even considered righteous among the nations.

However, for Jews, who received the Torah at Sinai, Christianity is forbidden as a foreign religion, and there is no sin and calamity more terrible for a Jew than converting to another religion, and the bitter memory of forced conversion to Christianity is still seared into the Jewish soul. Therefore, although the attitude toward Christians who have renounced hatred of Israel has changed, the laws of keeping away from churches remain in force.3

sections.title: Entering a Mosque and the Baha'i Gardens
sections.html:
According to the overwhelming majority of poskim, Islam is not idolatry (above 7, n. 1), and therefore from this aspect there is no prohibition to enter a mosque, and some wrote that in a time of need it is even permitted to pray inside it.

However, it seems that in practice it is forbidden nowadays to enter a mosque. This is because in recent generations many Muslims have become leaders of hatred of Israel in the world; they disgrace and degrade the people of Israel and its Torah, and in many mosques they stir up hatred of Israel, and in some they even call for war against Israel and the Jews. And the Sages said (Sifrei Zuta, Bamidbar 10:35): "Whoever is an enemy and hater of Israel is as if he is an enemy and hater of the Omnipresent." This is what is stated: "When the Ark set out, Moshe said: Arise, O Lord, and let Your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate You flee before You" (Bamidbar 10:35) – Your enemies and those who hate You are the enemies and haters of Israel. And about them it is stated: "Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and do I not quarrel with those who rise up against You? I hate them with utmost hatred; they have become my enemies" (Tehillim 139:21-22). The Sages also said (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael), on the verse "And in the greatness of Your majesty You overthrow those who rise against You" (Shemot 15:7) – who are those who rise up against God? "Whoever rises up against Israel is as if he rises up against the Holy One, blessed be He." Therefore, it is forbidden to enter an ordinary mosque. However, it is permitted to enter mosques that have good leaders who declare openly that they respect Israel and Judaism. And one who wishes to rely on those who permit may enter an ordinary mosque, provided that the mosque is not known for giving a platform to hatred of Israel.4

It is permitted to enter the place in the Cave of Makhpela where the Muslims pray, and it is permitted to hold prayers there as is customary. And although the Muslims established a mosque there, they entered our domain, the burial place of our forefathers and foremothers, and when we enter the Cave of Makhpela we are not entering a mosque, but visiting the graves of our holy forefathers and foremothers.

It is permitted to enter the Baha'i Gardens in Haifa, because their faith is not idolatry, but a stream that emerged from Islam and believes in one God. Likewise, it is permitted to enter their houses of prayer, because they respect the people of Israel and its religion, and recognise its right to the Land of Israel.5

sections.title: Entering a Church or Houses of Worship for Various Needs
sections.html:
As we learned (above 11:8), it is forbidden to build the room in which the worship of the various religions is held, because it is an accessory of idolatry. But the other rooms may be built, because they are tashmish de-tashmish (an accessory of an accessory). However, once the building is already being used as a place of worship, it is forbidden to enter even for renovations to a tashmish de-tashmish, because of mar'it ayin. But if two Jews enter together in work clothes, there is no concern of mar'it ayin, and they may carry out renovations in places defined as tashmish de-tashmish.

When a ballot box for elections is set up in rooms in a church building, the custom is to be lenient and enter there to vote, since it is clear that one is entering there not for the sake of idolatry. Similarly, a transport driver who in the course of his work must bring food and gentile pupils to schools that operate in churches may enter there in the course of his work.

Medical personnel who have been summoned to a house of idolatry or a church to give treatment to a patient must hurry to get there to treat the patient, for everyone knows that their aim is to save a person and not to draw near to idolatry. Likewise, police officers in charge of public order may, on idolatrous or Christian festival days, guard those gathered, since it is clear that their aim is to keep public order and to prevent crime.6

sections.title: Entering for Courtesy or for National Needs
sections.html:
It is forbidden to take part in a funeral service or a wedding held in a church. When it concerns the funeral of a work colleague, where courtesy requires one to share in the family's grief, one should take part in events that have no religious character, such as a condolence visit to their home before or after the funeral, or walking behind the coffin when there are no religious expressions there.

In a pressing situation, for a particularly great public need, such as ceremonies of the British royal family, the custom has been to permit representatives of the Jewish community to take part, since everyone knows that they are taking part out of public duty and not because of the religious aspect of the ceremony. And this was the practice of the Chief Rabbis of Britain.7

sections.title: Tourism
sections.html:
Even as part of a tourist trip it is forbidden to enter active churches and idolatrous temples, such as the temples found in the countries of the East. Likewise, it is forbidden to watch idolatrous rituals. Likewise, it is forbidden to enter a church in order to look at famous works of art, such as the churches in Rome and Venice. And although one who enters them is not suspected of intending to worship idolatry, one who enters there pays honour to it, contrary to the Torah's command (below 14:1); all the more so it is forbidden to enter and gaze at it and its ornaments. In addition, taking an interest in idolatry is also forbidden by Torah law, as it is stated: "Do not turn to the idols" (Vayikra 19:4).8

Jews should keep away from watching events of foreign religions, even when there is no idolatry in them, such as Muslim worship ceremonies or the Samaritan Pesaḥ sacrifice, as it is stated: "Keep your way far from her, and do not come near the door of her house" (Mishlei 5:8).

Tour guides are permitted to guide Christians who come to tour the Land and to enter churches with them, because there is a great need for this; for otherwise, haters of Israel will guide them and lead them into the sin of hating Israel. By contrast, when loyal Jewish guides guide them, they can awaken in the hearts of the tourists respect and love for Israel. However, when the tourists hold religious ceremonies, the guides must distance themselves from the group, and the rest of the time they should treat the tourists and the good aspect of their faith with respect.9

A house of idolatry that has been abandoned by its worshippers and deserted, and likewise an ancient house of idolatry uncovered in archaeological excavations – since it has ceased to be a house of idolatry, it is permitted to enter it for the purpose of studying history and the like. It is proper for those who look at a defunct house of idolatry to reflect on the great influence of Israel, by virtue of whose faith in the One God many forms of idolatry have ceased from the world. For this purpose the Sages instituted a blessing, as explained below in section 15.

It is permitted to look at idols or fragments of idols found in archaeological excavations, and likewise visitors to a museum may view idols and their fragments, because it is permitted to benefit from idols that have been nullified.10

sections.title: Donating to the Construction of a Church
sections.html:
Sometimes Jews who lived among the gentiles were asked, like the other residents of the town, to help with donations to the construction of the church. Sometimes there was danger in refusing to donate, and sometimes the church was led by lovers of Israel, and refusing to donate might harm the good relations with them. The poskim disagree on whether it is permitted, for the sake of darkhei shalom (the ways of peace), to donate to the construction of a church.

Rav Mordekhai Horowitz of Frankfurt wrote (Matteh Levi 2:28) that from early generations the custom has been to be lenient in this because of hostility and darkhei shalom, since Noahides were not commanded regarding shituf, and therefore they have no prohibition of idolatry in Christianity (above 5:10), and consequently there is no prohibition for a Jew to assist them in it. In his opinion, this donation even involves a sanctification of God's Name, for all the peoples of the earth will see that although we are faithful Jews, ready to give our lives with love for the faith in the One God, so that if a Jew is coerced to convert to Christianity he must be killed rather than convert, Noahides can accept Christianity and be among the pious and great of the nations of the world, and inherit the World to Come if they keep the seven Noahide commandments, and we are ready to help them in this. However, if there is an apostate Jew in their community who will enter there, it is forbidden (and so writes Rav Unna in She'elin Ve-dorshin 35). About a hundred years later, in 5756, Rav Shalom Mashash, chief rabbi of Morocco and afterwards of Jerusalem, relied on his words and permitted donating to churches in the United States that had been burned by haters of religion (Shemesh U-magen vol. 3, OḤ 30-31).

However, according to Rav David Tzvi Hoffmann, head of the Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin, it is forbidden for a Jew to donate to the construction of a church. And although according to most poskim Christianity is permitted to gentiles, since for Jews it is forbidden as idolatry, it is forbidden for a Jew to donate to its construction (Melamed Le-ho'il YD 148:2). However, when there is no choice, when there is concern about hostility, then even according to those who hold that shituf and Christianity are forbidden to gentiles, it is permitted to donate with the intention that the donation be for the construction of a tashmish de-tashmish of the place of worship, such as the entrance rooms and the courtyard, which, as we learned (above 11:8), a Jew is permitted to build. If possible, in order to ensure that the donation goes toward building a tashmish de-tashmish, he should donate the building materials needed for this (see Minḥat Shai 62).11

As for a mosque, although Muslims are not idolaters, since their leaders generally preach hatred of Israel, there is a mitzva to keep away from them, and it is forbidden to assist them. However, if it is known that they respect Israel and its religion, it is permitted to donate to them.

sections.title: A Cross for Worship Is Forbidden; as a Symbol It Is Permitted
sections.html:
According to most poskim, a cross intended for worship, to which people pray and bow, is considered idolatry, whereas a cross not intended for worship but as a symbol is not considered idolatry. Therefore, a cross that is set up in places of worship and to which people bow is considered idolatry and is forbidden for benefit; it is forbidden for a Jew to make it, and one who makes it is liable to lashes, as it is stated: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness" (Shemot 20:4) (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:9). Likewise, it is forbidden by Torah law to adorn it with decorations (ibid. 3:6).

On the other hand, a cross intended only as a symbol, to which people do not bow, is not considered idolatry and is not forbidden for benefit. Therefore, the crosses on the flags of countries, such as the flags of Britain, Switzerland and Sweden, since they are intended as a symbol and an identity and not for worship, are not considered idolatry, and it is permitted to manufacture them. Likewise, it is permitted to hang them in preparation for state visits. Similarly, medals and decorations of honour that kingdoms awarded, even though a cross appears at their centre, and sometimes they were even called a "cross of knighthood," since they were not intended for worship but for honour and recognition, there is no prohibition to receive them and to wear them for the sake of honour. The same law applies to stamps that bear a cross: it is permitted to use them and even to collect them.

However, it is proper for Jews to keep away from using decorations that recall foreign religions. Especially when entering a synagogue, it is proper to avoid wearing medals or clothes bearing symbols that recall a foreign religion. Likewise, regarding vessels decorated with a cross: since they were intended for ornament and not for people to bow to them, the vessels are permitted for benefit. However, the more recognisable the crosses are as expressing a foreign religion, the more preferable it is not to use them, or alternatively to erase the cross or conceal it. But crosses that are not recognisable as expressing a foreign religion but rather as a sign, such as those on the flags of countries, and such as those on chess pieces and other games, need not be removed.12

sections.title: Crosses Not Known to Have Been Worshipped
sections.html:
Vessels or objects that bear a cross, if they are items on which it is degrading to place an image for religious worship, such as coins and eating utensils – since it is known that they are not worshipped, there is no prohibition in them. Likewise, we find that in the days of the Sages they used coins on which images of idols were stamped (Shabbat 149a, Tosafot ad loc., s.v. "Ve-diyokni"; Ravya).13

The poskim disagree about one whose livelihood is making tombstones, many of whose customers are Christians who ask that a cross be made on the tombstone. According to the lenient view, since this cross is made for honour and not for worship, the Jewish business owner may instruct a gentile worker to make it. According to the stringent view, since this cross is made for honour, and believing Christians bow when they see it, through this bowing it becomes idolatry; therefore it is forbidden to benefit from it, and it is forbidden for a Jew to instruct a gentile worker to make it in order to profit from it.14

sections.title: A Cross on a Chain
sections.html:
The poskim disagree regarding a cross hung on a chain around the neck as an ornament. Some were stringent, because sometimes a Christian who wishes to pray sets this cross up before him and bows to it (Me'il Tzedaka). But according to many it is not considered idolatry and is permitted for benefit, because it is made as a remembrance, to express religious identity, and not for worship (Ravya; Rema YD 141:1). Therefore, a Jew who received in payment of a debt owed to him a gold cross adorned with precious stones may sell it. Similarly, a souvenir-shop owner who needs to sell, among other things, crosses that are worn around the neck may stock them and sell them.

When meeting a priest who wears a large priest's cross, one must take care not to bow before him, since the cross in the church is a form to which people bow, and if the Jew bows before the priest he will appear to be bowing to idolatry. He should also take care not to rise before him, so as not to appear to be honouring idolatry. However, in a pressing situation, when it concerns a priest with governmental status and refraining from bowing involves danger, they permitted bowing, since after all the bow is to the man and not to the cross. In addition, the cross he wears is not considered idolatry, since it is meant to express his status and office and not for worship. And there were priests who treated Jews with respect, and before meeting them would hide the cross they wore, so that the Jews could honour them with a bow, as was customary, without concern (Terumat Ha-deshen 196).

Ideally, one should not allow a gentile wearing a cross to enter the synagogue. Even if he needs to enter the synagogue to carry out maintenance work or to care for a sick person, one should ask him not to wear a cross. But if this might cause offence, one should not remark on it, because the view of most poskim is that a cross worn around the neck is not idolatry.

When distinguished gentiles, public and religious leaders, are invited to a synagogue for a prayer for the welfare of the state, or in support of the State of Israel, or for a rabbi's installation ceremony, ideally one should ask them not to wear a cross. But if they decided to wear a cross, one should not remark on it, so as not to cause offence.15

sections.title: Hospitals and Lodgings That Contain Images
sections.html:
It is permitted to enter buildings that are not houses of idolatry, even though they contain images or crosses that are venerated, because the building as a whole was not intended for idolatry. All the more so one may enter there when the images placed there were intended for ornament and not for worship (SA YD 142:14). And so is the custom in America and Europe, that Jews enter hospitals and places containing crosses and icons. If the building has a room designated for worship, it is forbidden to enter that room (Masoret Moshe vol. 2, pp. 192-193).

Similarly, in a time of need it is permitted to stay overnight in a lodging that contains an image that idolaters venerate by bowing, placing offerings and burning incense, since the lodging as a whole is not considered a house of idolatry. Ideally, one should not pray in a room containing an idolatrous image or picture, in the manner of what Moshe our teacher said: "As soon as I go out of the city, I will spread out my hands to the Lord" (Shemot 9:29). The Sages explained that Moshe did not want to pray in the city, which was full of idols (Shemot Rabba 12:5).

And if he has no other place to pray except a room containing an image, he should pray there, taking care not to pray and bow facing the image (Rema OḤ 94:9; MB 30). Even when reciting blessings, it is right for him to turn his face away from the image.

There is no prohibition to bathe in a bathhouse or to use a hall in which idolatrous images or pictures were placed as ornament. And although in places designated for worship people bow to those images and pictures, in places where they were placed for ornament it is permitted to use them. And so the Mishna relates about Rabban Gamliel, who bathed in a bathhouse in which a statue of the goddess Aphrodite was set up as an ornament, and when he was asked about it, he replied: "I did not come into her domain; she came into my domain. One does not say: The bathhouse was made as an ornament for Aphrodite; rather one says: Aphrodite was made as an ornament for the bathhouse." Moreover, it is not set up there in a respectful manner, for everyone goes about their business there without regard for its honour (Avoda Zara 44b; SA YD 142:14). However, ideally, when possible, it is right to keep away from a place where one is compelled to look at pictures of idolatry.

sections.title: The Blessing on Seeing Idolatry
sections.html:
Although the Sages instructed us to keep away from idolatry, if a Jew is compelled to pass near it, he must recite a blessing on seeing it: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has given patience to those who transgress His will" (SA OḤ 224:1). And although it is forbidden to turn to idols by gazing at idolatry, the prohibition is to look at length in order to contemplate it, but there is no prohibition in a brief glance. The purpose of this blessing is to direct our minds to the fact that although God rules over all and is able to destroy all forms of idolatry, He gave man free choice and is patient with those who transgress His will, who imagine that various idols govern the world, so that they may repent and choose to believe in God.

The blessing is recited on seeing images that are venerated, but one who sees a building containing idolatrous images should not recite the blessing (Baḥ). If he sees the same image again within thirty days, he does not recite the blessing; if thirty days have passed, he recites it. And even if thirty days have not passed, if he sees a different image, even of the same kind, he recites the blessing.

Those who live among idolaters and are used to seeing their images do not recite the blessing on seeing them, even if in practice they have not seen them for thirty days, because seeing them is routine for them and holds nothing new (Rema OḤ 224:1; Eliyahu Rabba; MB 3). But if they see images of another religion to which they are not accustomed, they recite the blessing.

It seems that because of the doubt, one should not recite the blessing on the images of those who worship idolatry with shituf, that is, who also believe in the One God, who is above the idols, as most idolaters today do.16

sections.title: The Blessing on a Place from Which Idolatry Has Been Uprooted
sections.html:
One who sees a place from which idolatry has been uprooted recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has uprooted idolatry from our land." Outside the Land, one concludes: "from this place." After the blessing one says: "Just as You have uprooted it from this place, so may You uproot it from all places, and turn the hearts of their worshippers to serve You." It is worth noting that we pray for all Noahides, that they will repent and serve God, and therefore we say: "and turn the hearts of their worshippers to serve You."

Idolatry that was uprooted from one place and moved to another place: over the place from which it was uprooted one recites the blessing on its nullification, and over the place where it still exists one recites "who has given patience to those who transgress His will" (SA and Rema OḤ 224:2).

It is proper for tour guides to include sites where there were ancient idolatrous cults that have since been nullified, and to describe to the travellers how in the past their worshippers were certain that they would continue to worship them forever, and in the end, through the influence of the faith of Israel, this idolatry ceased from the world; and afterwards they should all recite the blessing together (see Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 15:16).
